scope: Literature-based systematic budget for multiplicity / companion blending. NO end-to-end crossmatch of our hosts to the El-Badry+21 bound-pair catalog was performed.

crossmatch_status.detail: The frozen data contain gaia_hosts_M.csv with 301 unique Gaia DR3 source_ids covering 301 of the 303 M-dwarf host names (Kepler-1410 and Kepler-1652 are absent). The El-Badry+21 bound-pair catalog is not present in the frozen data and was not downloaded, so no source_id1/source_id2 lookup was run and no sample-specific binary fraction is claimed.

sources.citation: Bergsten et al. (2026), arXiv:2601.16031, 'Modeling the Impact of Unresolved Stellar Companions on Detection Sensitivity in Kepler's Small Planet Occurrence Rates' (draft 2026-01-23)
sources.sample: 198 Kepler stars with Earth-like-planet sensitivity, AO-imaged; 40 systems with close companions = 20% unresolved companion rate; field rate used as upper limit = 45%

effects.effect: unresolved-companion occurrence correction, all small planets (1-3.5 R_E, 2-100 d)
effects.magnitude: 1.08 (+0.14/-0.12) observed treatment; 1.18 (+0.17/-0.14) field treatment; abstract range 1.08-1.19
effects.quote: Median occurrence rates for small planets between 2-100 days increased by an average factor of 1.08-1.19 (depending on statistical treatments), with the largest differences found for smaller planets at larger orbital periods.
effects.direction_on_beta: Upward bias on small-planet occurrence, concentrated in super-Earths at long period; can inflate SN fraction of the older/longer-period population and bias the raw age contrast upward.

effects.magnitude: Table 1 occurrence ratios span 1.06 (minimum) to 1.24 (maximum); super-Earths 1.10 vs sub-Neptunes 1.06; at long period 1.24 vs 1.13; Savel+2020 71-star precedent 1.06 Earth-like / 1.26 super-Earths+sub-Neptunes
effects.quote: with a factor of 1.26 increase for super-earths and sub-Neptunes
effects.direction_on_beta: Period-dependent, not age-dependent: acts mainly on the period-mixing component of the signal; no evidence it discriminates old from young hosts at fixed period.

effects.effect: Kepler completeness/reliability products ignore unresolved-companion blending
effects.magnitude: systematic in the published completeness maps; 20% (observed) to 45% (field) companion-rate treatments
effects.quote: the construction of the Kepler occurrence rate products (e.g., the Kepler candidate list, the completeness, and the reliability products) do not take into account the blending of nearby companions
effects.direction_on_beta: Under-corrected detectability for multi-star hosts; sign of the net bias on our beta depends on the (unmeasured) age dependence of companion incidence.

sources.applies_to: FGK control sample (the sample that carries the +4.14 pp residual AME), but no companion classification exists in our frozen files

sources.citation: Messamah, Bouchy, Venturini, Parc & Nigioni (2026), A&A manuscript aa59086-26, arXiv:2605.31523v2, 'Mind the companion: Demographics of transiting S-type exoplanets'
sources.sample: PlanetS catalogue 860 transiting planets; 133 S-type planets in Gaia-DR3 bound binaries (El-Badry+21 crossmatch), projected separations 76-9655 AU, 552-planet matched single-star control

effects.magnitude: 19.4% relative to matched control; 15.5% relative to full single sample; field-star binary fraction ~11% (13148/118650)
effects.quote: We find a binary fraction of 19.4% relative to the control sample (15.5% relative to the full single-star sample), consistent with previous estimates but derived from a larger and more homogeneous dataset.
effects.direction_on_beta: If companion incidence differs between our old and young host subsets, it can change the effective detectability and radius classification; direction unknown without an age-resolved count.

effects.effect: giant planets around M dwarfs in binaries
effects.magnitude: ~50% of M-dwarf giant planets in binaries (2.6 sigma excess vs FGK); field M-dwarf value 12.2+/-0.4%; 55.6% of M-dwarf companions within 1000 AU
effects.quote: In particular, we derive that ~50% of giant planets orbiting M-dwarfs are in binary systems, predominantly with separations < 1000 AU, a 2.6 sigma excess compared to FGK-type hosts
effects.direction_on_beta: Giant-planet regime only; our M-dwarf sample is small planets (0.5-4 R_E), so this is contextual, not a direct systematic on beta.

effects.effect: small planets: no significant spectral-type dependence of binary fraction
effects.magnitude: no statistically significant difference; limited statistics; only resolved S-type binaries (tighter unresolved systems explicitly excluded)
effects.quote: In contrast, the small planet regime shows no statistically significant difference in binary fraction across stellar spectral types, although current statistics remain limited.
effects.direction_on_beta: Reassuring for the M-dwarf small-planet gate: no evidence of a large spectral-type-dependent multiplicity bias in the regime we use, but unresolved companions are out of scope here.

sources.applies_to: both M-dwarf science sample and FGK control, via literature only

sources.citation: Sullivan et al. (2023), arXiv:2302.08532v1, 'There is No Observed Radius Gap For Kepler Planets in Binary Star Systems' (draft 2023-02-20)
sources.sample: 119 planet-host binary stars; 122 planets in binaries around primary stars

effects.effect: no significant radius gap in binary-host planets
effects.magnitude: no statistically significant radius gap; AD-test p<0.05 against consistency with the single-star small-planet population
effects.quote: We found no statistically significant evidence for a radius gap for our sample of 122 planets in binaries when assuming the primary stars are the planet hosts, with a low probability (p < 0.05) of the binary planet sample radius distribution being consistent with the single-star small planet population via an Anderson-Darling test.
effects.direction_on_beta: Binary hosts can blur or remove the valley; if binaries are more common in one age bin, the valley-based AME is diluted toward zero.

effects.effect: undetected multiplicity shrinks apparent planet radii
effects.magnitude: qualitative, not quantified for our sample
effects.quote: Binaries cause observational biases in planet parameters, with undetected multiplicity causing transiting planets to appear smaller than they truly are.
effects.direction_on_beta: Flux dilution moves planets across the radius gate from sub-Neptune to super-Earth; sign on the SN excess depends on which age group is more blended.

sources.citation: Sullivan et al. (2024), arXiv:2406.17648v1, 'The Radius Distribution of Small Planets in Binary Star Systems is Dependent on Stellar Separation' (draft 2024-06-26)
sources.sample: 207 binary systems hosting 283 confirmed and candidate transiting Kepler planets, recharacterized for secondary-star bias

effects.effect: close binaries show unimodal, super-Earth-peaked radius distribution
effects.magnitude: close binaries (a <~ 100 au) unimodal, peak Rp ~ 1.3 R_E, suppressed sub-Neptunes; distinct from wider binaries (>300 au) and single stars
effects.quote: In contrast to planets around single stars, planets in close binaries appear to have a unimodal radius distribution with a peak near the expected super-Earth peak of Rp ~ 1.3 R_E and a suppressed population of sub-Neptunes.
effects.direction_on_beta: If close binaries were more common among older hosts, they would raise the old-host super-Earth fraction and bias the AME upward; if more common among younger hosts, downward. Our frozen data contain no separation-resolved binary flag.

sources.citation: El-Badry, Rix & Heintz (2021), MNRAS 000, 1-26, 'A million binaries from Gaia eDR3: sample selection and validation of Gaia parallax uncertainties'
sources.sample: Gaia eDR3 bound-pair catalog within ~1 kpc; projected separations a few au to 1 pc

effects.effect: catalog size and bound-probability completeness (enabler, not a bias on beta itself)
effects.magnitude: 1.3 million pairs with >90% bound probability; 1.1 million with >99% bound probability; 16,000 WD+MS and 1,400 WD+WD pairs
effects.quote: The catalog contains 1.3 (1.1) million binaries with >90% (>99%) probability of being bound, including 16,000 white dwarf - main sequence (WD+MS) binaries and 1,400 WD+WD binaries.
effects.direction_on_beta: Enables a future crossmatch; no direct effect on beta without applying it to our hosts.

effects.magnitude: all pairs with projected separations >10,000 AU have chance-alignment probability >0.01 and are excluded
effects.quote: Essentially, all pairs with projected separations greater than 10, 000 AU have chance-alignment probabilities > 0.01; therefore, no robustly bound wide binaries are excluded by this criterion.
effects.direction_on_beta: Sets the reliability floor for any companion classification; does not itself bias beta.

bottom_line.bergsten_detectability_range: 1.06-1.24 occurrence ratio (6-24% relative), largest for super-Earths at long period
bottom_line.verdict: The 6-24% period-dependent detectability differential is NOT sufficient to account for the +4.14 pp residual AME: it is period-dependent (the component already conditioned out), not age-dependent, and the largest companion-rate contrast quoted in the literature (20% observed vs 45% field = 25 pp) predicts only ~0.6-2.4 pp on a ~0.4 super-Earth fraction, and that only under the untested assumption that the 45% treatment applies exclusively to the older hosts. Explaining +4.14 pp outright would require an age-differential companion incidence of 43-173 pp, which is unphysical at the low-correction end and implausible at the high-correction end.
